common_name: Bola de Oro Chrysanthemum (Golden Irregular Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; like other irregular incurve exhibition types, Bola de Oro is grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a multi-stemmed garden clump.

directions: Bola de Oro is an irregular incurve exhibition chrysanthemum, the giant 'football mum' class prized by National Chrysanthemum Society exhibitors for its dense, globe-shaped bloom built from hundreds of inward-curving golden-yellow florets that completely hide the center. Grow it as a single disbudded stem: pinch the young plant once in late spring to set the bud count, then remove every side bud as it appears so the plant channels its energy into one terminal flower, and stake the stem early since the finished bloom is heavy enough to topple an unsupported plant. Root fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter rather than relying on an old clump, since exhibition-quality bloom size depends on vigorous young growth, and overwinter stock under cover in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse where winters are harsh.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Chrysanthemum Classification Guide

common_name: Hagoromo Chrysanthemum (Classic White Japanese Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Hagoromo is a Japanese heritage incurve type maintained through annual cutting propagation rather than left as an undisturbed garden clump.

directions: Hagoromo is a large irregular incurve exhibition chrysanthemum of Japanese heritage, its name borrowed from the classical Noh play about a celestial feathered robe, fitting for a bloom whose densely overlapping creamy-white florets curve inward in soft, feather-like layers. As with other football-type exhibition mums, discipline the plant to a single stem by pinching once in late spring and removing all but the terminal bud so remaining energy goes into one large, well-formed flower, providing a sturdy stake well before the bud swells. Propagate annually from basal cuttings taken off overwintered stock in late winter, since repeated division of old clumps tends to produce smaller, less symmetrical blooms than fresh cuttings.

common_name: Mt. Shasta Chrysanthemum (Large White Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Mt. Shasta is grown as a single disbudded stem in the classic irregular incurve exhibition style.

directions: Mt. Shasta is an irregular incurve exhibition mum named for the snow-capped California peak, its tightly packed, inward-rolling florets opening a pure glacial white that lives up to the name. Like other football-type exhibition chrysanthemums, it is grown as a single disbudded stem: pinch once in late spring to establish bud sites, then strip away every side bud except the terminal one so the plant's full vigor goes into one outsized bloom, staking early to support the eventual weight of the flower head. Take basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter for the next season's crop, and shelter overwintering stock in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse where winters are harsh, since this class is maintained through annual propagation rather than left as a permanent garden clump.

common_name: Woolmans Century Chrysanthemum (Heritage British Incurve Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Woolmans Century traces to the Woolman line of British exhibition chrysanthemum raisers.

directions: Woolmans Century carries the name of the Woolman family, a long line of British exhibition chrysanthemum raisers, and produces the dense, globe-shaped irregular incurve bloom their introductions are known for. Grow it as a disbudded single stem in the classic exhibition style: pinch once in late spring to set branching, then remove every side bud but the terminal one so all of the plant's energy builds one large, tightly formed flower, staking the stem well ahead of bud swell since the finished bloom is top-heavy. Because exhibition-quality size comes from vigorous first-year growth, take fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter rather than dividing an aging clump, and keep stock plants under cover through winter in regions where the ground freezes hard.

common_name: Evening Glow Chrysanthemum (Amber Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Evening Glow is a spider-type exhibition mum grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a bushy garden clump.

directions: Evening Glow is a spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum, its narrow, tubular florets radiating outward and curling or hooking at the tips in the loose, spidery form that gives the class its name, in warm amber-bronze tones that deepen as the bloom ages. Train it as a single disbudded stem, pinching once in late spring and removing all but the terminal bud so the plant commits its full energy to one large flower, and stake it early since the long, outward-splaying florets make the bloom head catch wind easily. Propagate from basal cuttings taken off stock plants each late winter for the strongest bloom the following fall, and overwinter stock under cover in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse in cold-winter regions rather than leaving plants in open ground.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Icicles is a spider-type exhibition mum grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a bushy garden clump.

directions: Icicles is a spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum whose long, thin, pure white florets droop and curl at the tips, giving the finished bloom the dangling, icy look its name suggests. Grow it as a single disbudded stem, pinching once in late spring to set the framework and then removing every side bud but the terminal one so the plant's energy is concentrated into one large bloom; stake early, since the narrow, elongated florets of spider types are easily disturbed by wind and rain. Root new basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter rather than relying on an old clump, and protect overwintering stock from hard freezes under cover in cold climates.

common_name: Golden Splendor Chrysanthemum (Golden Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Golden Splendor is a spider-type exhibition mum grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a bushy garden clump.

directions: Golden Splendor is a spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum with long, thin golden-yellow florets that curl and hook at the tips, building a loose, radiating bloom quite different from the tight daisy or button forms of garden mums. As with other exhibition disbuds, pinch the young plant once in late spring to establish branching, then remove all side buds except the terminal one so the plant's energy goes into a single oversized flower, staking well before the bud swells since spider blooms are top-heavy and easily wind-damaged. Take basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter for the next year's crop, overwintering stock under cover in regions with hard winters rather than leaving plants in the open garden.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Chesapeake is a spider-type exhibition mum grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a bushy garden clump.

directions: Chesapeake is a spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum, producing the long, thread-like florets that curl or hook at the tips characteristic of the class, built into a single large, loosely radiating bloom rather than the dense daisy or pompon heads of garden mums. Grow it as a disbudded single stem: pinch once in late spring to set branching, then strip away every side bud but the terminal one, and stake the stem early since the finished bloom's weight and spidery florets make it vulnerable to wind and rain. For best bloom size, take fresh basal cuttings from stock plants every late winter instead of dividing an older clump, and keep stock protected over winter in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse where the ground freezes hard.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Nightingale is a spider-type exhibition mum grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a bushy garden clump.

directions: Nightingale is a spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum grown for its long, slender florets that coil or hook at the tips, forming a loose, airy bloom very different in form from garden-type daisy or button mums. Discipline the plant to a single stem in classic exhibition style, pinching once in late spring and removing every side bud but the terminal one so all of the plant's vigor builds one large flower, staking well ahead of bud swell since the elongated florets are easily knocked about by weather. Propagate from basal cuttings taken off overwintered stock plants each late winter, and shelter stock under cover through the coldest months in regions where it would not reliably survive left in open ground.

directions: Zaryah is a spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum, its narrow tubular florets radiating outward and curling at the tips to form the loose, spidery bloom typical of the class rather than the compact daisy or cushion forms common in garden mums. Grow it as a single disbudded stem, pinching once in late spring to establish the plant's framework and then removing all side buds but the terminal one so its energy concentrates into one large flower; stake the stem early, since spider-type blooms are heavy and their long florets catch wind easily. Take basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter rather than dividing an aging clump, and protect stock plants over winter under cover in regions with hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Kimie is a spoon-type exhibition mum grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a bushy garden clump.

directions: Kimie is a spoon-type exhibition chrysanthemum, a form that looks much like a single daisy-flowered mum except that each petal-like floret is tubular for most of its length and flares open into a small flattened spoon at the tip, giving the bloom a distinctive studded texture. Pinch the young plant once in late spring to establish branching, then disbud to a single terminal flower per stem in the standard exhibition style, staking as the bud develops since even spoon-type blooms can be top-heavy on a single stem. Propagate from basal cuttings taken off stock plants each late winter for the most vigorous bloom, and overwinter stock under cover rather than leaving plants in open ground in cold-winter climates.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Oriental Knight is a spoon-type exhibition mum grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a bushy garden clump.

directions: Oriental Knight is a spoon-type exhibition chrysanthemum, its florets tubular along most of their length and flattened into a small spoon shape at the tip, giving the open bloom a textured, almost beaded look distinct from flat single daisies or dense incurve forms. Grow it as a disbudded single stem: pinch once in late spring to set branching, then remove every side bud but the terminal one so the plant's energy builds one well-formed flower, staking the stem as the bud swells. As with other exhibition types, take fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter rather than relying on an old clump, and keep stock plants protected over winter in a cold frame or unheated greenhouse in harsher climates.

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Whirlaway is a spoon-type exhibition mum grown as a single disbudded stem rather than a bushy garden clump.

directions: Whirlaway is a spoon-type exhibition chrysanthemum whose florets stay narrow and tubular for most of their length before flaring into a small rounded spoon at the tip, giving the bloom an airy, pinwheel-like texture compared with flat-petaled daisy mums. Pinch the young plant once in late spring to establish framework, then disbud down to a single terminal flower per stem as is standard for exhibition culture, staking the stem as the bud develops to keep the finished bloom upright. Take basal cuttings from stock plants each late winter to propagate the next season's crop, and overwinter stock under cover in regions where plants left in the open garden would not reliably survive.
